title: What drives our behaviors in buildings? A review on occupant interactions with building systems from the lens of behavioral theories
review_question: 1. Identifying the psychological, sociological, economic theories and their associated elements (constructs) that have been applied to understand interactions of occupants with one or multiple building energy systems; 2. Understanding to what extent these theories have been leveraged in the literature to characterize occupants' interactions with building systems; 3. Providing a review of research methods that have been applied to conduct such studies; 4. Identifying the characteristics of such studies including the geographical locations, types of buildings, number of participants, and their findings; 5. Discussing the existing research gaps and roadmap for future research in this area.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included studies were guided by a behavioral theory, applying one or more such theories to understand or predict interaction with at least one building system, or used at least one psychological, sociological, or economic factor to predict/explain occupant interactions with building systems. Excluded studies did not explicitly examine/provide data on behavioral factors' influence on occupant interaction with energy-related building systems, were reviews, examined purchase of energy-efficient appliances, focused on feedback mechanisms without behavioral insights, or focused on physiological factors/intervention strategies to reduce energy consumption.

synthesis_conclusions: The review categorized behavioral theories applied to explain occupant behavior and interactions with major building systems.
The current state and challenges in understanding driving factors for occupant behaviors in residential and non-residential buildings from an applied theoretical perspective were identified.
The majority of existing research focuses on a few well-known behavioral theories: Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), Value Belief Norm, Norm Activation Model, and Social Practice Theory.
Compared to psychological theories, significantly fewer studies investigate how sociological and economic theories explain occupant behavior and interactions with different building systems.
Among sociological theories, Social Practice Theory and Energy Cultures were more commonly studied, with very few economic theories in the literature.
evidence_gaps: Limited number of studies have examined different behavioral theories and predictors in understanding occupant interactions with HVAC systems.
Need for a greater understanding of how socio-psychological-economic factors influence behaviors in isolation and in combination with thermophysiological drivers.
Majority of identified studies are purely self-reported, lacking experimental and naturalistic studies in real-world environments.
More studies should be conducted in different geographical locations to better capture behavioral differences in HVAC system interactions.
Limited number of studies have examined different behavioral theories and predictors in understanding occupant window openings and ventilation behavior.
Many identified studies neglected the influence of environmental factors such as indoor/outdoor temperature or indoor air quality on window opening/closing behavior.
Studies need to be better designed by focusing on a specific behavioral theory, ensuring all constructs are explicitly considered and accounted for.
Relationship between experimental design and specific theories/constructs was not clearly explained in some studies.
More studies are needed in different countries as various geographical locations and cultural differences may significantly influence lighting and shading behaviors.
Predominant model (TPB and Habits) should be applied more coherently instead of scattered constructs.
Reliance on self-reported intentions versus actual measured savings (Attitude-Behavior-Gap) is a limitation.
Need for longer baseline measurements and follow-up observation periods in intervention studies.
More research is needed to understand drivers of hot water heating related behaviors.
Lack of consistency in applying theories makes it difficult to draw consistent conclusions about hot water use drivers.
Small sample sizes in hot water studies limit generalizability.
More studies are needed in different geographical locations for hot water behavior, considering cultural and economic factors.
Opportunity to apply sociological and economic theories to enhance understanding of human interaction with commercial building systems.
Survey-based studies are most common, especially for psychological theories, while interview approaches for sociological theories, indicating disciplinary bias.
Need for research across a wider geographical spectrum, particularly in developing countries, to understand how cultural and demographic factors impact behaviors across building systems.
No common agreement on the influence of theories on mixed systems due to differences in location, sample, aims, and number of buildings.
Further research should focus on collecting real data and including control groups for validation purposes, moving beyond self-reported measures.
Researchers should move beyond commonly studied theories to explore less-commonly applied theories for occupant interactions with different building systems.
Future studies should incorporate a cleaner design to disentangle results in mixed systems studies.
Deeper dive into more nuanced behavioral theories is needed to understand occupant behavior and interactions with different building systems.
Greater need for close collaborations between technical and social disciplines.
Future studies should integrate measures from various fields (physiological data, productivity, health/well-being metrics) for a holistic understanding of occupant behaviors.
Research is needed on identifying approaches to conserve occupant security and privacy with new sensing technologies.
More studies are needed in extreme environments (e.g., Alaska) to identify factors for designing/operating future buildings and enhancing system adaptability.
Cultural and language differences must be considered in study design for international/cross-country research, including pre-test studies.
limitations: Limited empirical and naturalistic studies exist, with many reviewed studies conducted through surveys and questionnaires.
Questionnaires often used few single-item questions to examine psychological theories.
Surveys may not be sufficient to generalize how particular behavioral theories apply in specific contexts.
Studies are conducted over a short period of time with small sample sizes, limiting confidence in detecting proposed effects.
The majority of identified studies applied very few and well-known theories, which may not be the most appropriate for all occupant interactions.
Mixed systems studies, while realistic, can be difficult to disentangle results.
